issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s unauthorized occupation of accommodation outside the let premises is a distinct ground for eviction from making an unauthorized construction within the let premises, and eviction may follow when the tenant fails to comply with a direction to vacate the extra portion and pay compensation.
material_facts: The tenant occupied and constructed a shed or room on a portion not included in the accommodation let to him.
The trial court directed the tenant to vacate that portion and pay compensation, but the tenant did not comply with the direction; an undertaking to comply was also not fulfilled.
The first appellate court treated proof of diminished value or prejudice to the landlord as necessary, although those matters concern a different eviction ground.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court applied the wrong test. For unauthorized occupation of a portion not let to the tenant, the landlord need not prove that the occupation diminished the accommodation’s value or prejudiced the landlord; failure to comply with the direction to vacate and pay compensation can support eviction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12(1)(o) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 concerns unauthorized occupation of a portion not included in the let accommodation, without the landlord’s written permission and despite written notice to vacate. Read with Section 12(11), a tenant may avoid eviction on this ground by vacating the portion within the time specified by the court and paying the directed compensation; failure to comply can entail eviction. This ground is distinct from Section 12(1)(m), which concerns unauthorized construction or alteration within the let accommodation and requires material alteration to the landlord’s detriment or likely substantial diminution in value.

rule.if: eviction_suit and unauthorized_occupation_of_unlet_portion and no_written_permission and written_notice_to_vacate and court_directed_vacation_and_compensation and tenant_failed_to_comply_with_direction

predicates.eviction_suit: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.unauthorized_occupation_of_unlet_portion: The tenant occupied a portion of accommodation that was not included in the premises let to the tenant.
predicates.no_written_permission: The landlord had not given written permission for the tenant to occupy the additional portion.
predicates.written_notice_to_vacate: The landlord gave the tenant written notice to vacate the additional portion.
predicates.court_directed_vacation_and_compensation: The court directed the tenant to vacate the additional portion and pay compensation for it.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_comply_with_direction: The tenant did not comply with the court’s direction to vacate the portion and pay compensation.

issues.definition: When a tenant in an eviction proceeding occupies an unlet portion without written permission, does not vacate after written notice, and fails to comply with a court direction to vacate and pay compensation, eviction on that ground is permitted.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who fails to pay or deposit rent as required during an appeal cannot retain the statutory protection against eviction for rent default merely because the tenant earlier received that protection at trial.
material_facts: The trial court initially gave the tenant the benefit of the statutory protection against eviction for rent default after the rent was deposited following service of the suit.
During the landlord’s appeal, the landlord alleged that the tenant had not paid or deposited rent and applied to have the tenant’s defence struck out.
The tenant did not provide an acceptable explanation rebutting the allegation, and the High Court found that rent remained unpaid during the appeal.
The first appellate court had wrongly placed the burden on the landlord to prove non-payment and had treated payment during the appeal as unnecessary.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s defence against eviction should have been struck out for failure to pay or deposit rent during the appeal, and the first appellate court should have allowed the landlord’s appeal on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 12(1)(a) and 12(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Accommodation Control Act, 1961 govern eviction for rent default and the protection available to a tenant who complies with Section 13. Under Section 13(1), the tenant must pay or deposit the arrears within the applicable time and continue paying or depositing rent month by month during the suit, appeal, or other proceeding. Section 13(5) protects a compliant tenant from a possession decree on the default ground, while Section 13(6) permits the court to strike out the defence against eviction when the tenant fails to make required payments or deposits. The Court held on the unrebutted facts that the defence ought to have been struck out.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had failed to pay rent.
predicates.rent_required_during_appeal_was_not_paid: The tenant did not pay or deposit rent required during the pending appeal.
predicates.nonpayment_allegation_was_not_adequately: The tenant did not provide an acceptable explanation rebutting the allegation that the required rent had not been paid or deposited.

issues.definition: In a rent-default eviction proceeding, a tenant who fails to pay or deposit rent required during an appeal and does not adequately rebut the nonpayment allegation should have the defence against eviction struck out.

issues.legal_issue: In a second appeal, the High Court may determine a necessary issue of fact when the evidence is sufficient and the lower appellate court did not determine the issue or wrongly determined it because of an error on a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The landlord brought a second appeal after the first appellate court dismissed the landlord’s appeal.
The first appellate court failed to determine the relevant rent-payment and unauthorized-occupation issues because it applied erroneous legal approaches.
The evidence on the record was sufficient for the High Court to determine those issues.
issues.conclusion: The High Court acted within its jurisdiction in determining the relevant factual issues, and its judgment involved no illegality on that account.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 100 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure confine a second appeal to substantial questions of law and generally do not permit the High Court to revisit findings of fact. Section 103 permits the High Court, when the evidence is sufficient, to determine an issue of fact necessary to dispose of the appeal if the lower appellate court did not determine it, or if it was wrongly determined because of a decision on a substantial question of law. The Court relied on Afsar Sheikh v. Soeman Bibi and Jadu Gopal Chakravarty v. Pannalal Bhowmick.

rule.if: second_appeal and fact_issue_necessary_to_dispose_of_appeal and evidence_sufficient and (issue_not_determined_by_lower_appellate_court or issue_wrongly_determined_due_to_substantial_question_of_law)

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.fact_issue_necessary_to_dispose_of_appea: Determining the factual issue is necessary to dispose of the appeal.
predicates.evidence_sufficient: The record contains sufficient evidence to determine the factual issue.
predicates.issue_not_determined_by_lower_appellate_: The lower appellate court did not determine the factual issue.
predicates.issue_wrongly_determined_due_to_substant: The lower appellate court wrongly determined the factual issue because of its decision on a substantial question of law.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, the High Court may determine a necessary factual issue when the evidence is sufficient and the lower appellate court either did not determine it or wrongly determined it because of a substantial question of law.
